title: How to Market Yourself as a Personal Trainer (Without Going Viral)
paragraphs: Miles: So, the the next podcast guest we have on the PT Launch Lab podcast is none other than my old friend Josh. Josh from Axxis helps personal trainers with their branding, the systems, the social media, and he's we're lucky to have him now as part of PT Launch Lab helping graduates from the courses building a successful PT business. So because we go way back, Josh, I'll let you explain how you got into the industry.

Josh: Yeah, it's a good story as well. So obviously for those that are watching, obviously Miles was like my first mentor, boss. I started doing my level 2 as a gym instructor. First thing I wanted to do was just work in a gym. And obviously we started, for those of you who don't know, it's Sixfit, but to me it's always gonna be Strength 1. Is that the original name? Streamline Fitness, yeah, the original name, yeah, yeah. So on with you, roundabout, that's where I started, did my level 3, and really from there it was just working gym floor, doing the classes, just getting to know the members. And then I think obviously from there bounced around a couple of gyms from Bradford, still working on the, you know, personal training side, but it was really when we started getting into lockdown, eventually with social media, started building an online brand, and I think I was just Almost forced to go online, and that was where the online coaching side came into it.

Callum: What do you mean forced? This is an interesting question because when you say forced, was that just because of the times, or do you feel like that were the smartest move? Josh: I'd say smartest move as well, but I think a business can only grow as well as your skill sets allow. Obviously, if I was going back right now, then yeah, there was probably ways I could go around it, but back then I didn't really know. know too much about business, and just because gyms have been taken away, the only other viable option seems to be working online. Callum: Yeah, I think COVID was a great time for people to take that step. But do you find now that's changed a bit? Because when the gyms opened back up and people had different outlets and could go back to the gym, did that change or was it still on the rise?

Josh: I think COVID was a good thing because it pushed a lot of- it pushed all coaches' backs right up against the wall. And I think that environment- I literally remember having a conversation, seeing the stories. You'd see coaches sinking, you'd see coaches rising out of it. I think when your back's up against the wall, the only way you have is to either adapt or grow with it. And that is when there'll be certain coaches that make it, certain coaches that don't. Yeah, so Callum: yeah, it's- it's- I always love the idea of it and people getting My biggest question, I'm sure it'll come up today, is when PTs are qualifying, is it the smartest thing to go online?

Josh: I don't think so, no. Um, especially with the online coaching space not being regulated, it opens up the doors to a lot of snake oil salesmen. I see it all the time. You'll see, you know, your average guy get in really good shape, he steps on stage by having a bodybuilding coach. He then becomes a coach. And before you know it, you've got this guy as an online coach and he's got 30-year-old Susan on a 1.8K calorie diet and then she's peaking to go to a 9-to-5 job. Miles: And is he just copying and pasting what his coach has given him? Josh: Yeah, yeah, yeah. There's no, you know, aspect of the service delivery, tailoring it. Miles: It's just like blood and guts training. Josh: So I think, you know, being a personal trainer, just that reps in the game of working the gym floor is One of the best things that you can

Callum: do. Find out what you're actually good at as well. Because I think the copy and paste method, the ChatGPT method, even now with RetroTide that's on the market, a lot of trainers are using that in the background and posting these fantastic transformations and not being honest about it, saying, you know, they've achieved this in only 8 weeks. It's like, you're gonna see through smoke and mirrors eventually. But to people out there who don't know the game, it feels like it's almost Too good to be true.

Josh: Yeah. I think as well, the thing that is making a lot of PTs, coaches panic now with wondering where their next client is coming from is the actual market is so much more smaller. It used to be years ago, 2017, 2018, as a lead magnet, you could fling out a recipe book and you'd have 200 email subscribers just like that. Nowadays, you'd be surprised how many coaches struggle to sell something for free, let alone paid.

Miles: One thing I, you you can tell us your, your expert opinion on this, Josh. What I'm what I'm seeing is now is personal trainers not doing the authentic testimonials with clients anymore. Now, in a time when trust is lower than ever because of AI, because of people cheating with Retuxide, GLP meds to get the clients in shape, why do you think that clients aren't doing the old school Sitting down with a client, talking about the journey, how they started, where, with a real person. Why do you think people stopped doing that?

Josh: It's a good question. I think as well, part of that is down to everything being so accessible. I can literally open up that laptop, go on ChatGPT, and it will write me a business plan, it will write me content for the week. Everything is so accessible. So when we look at these old school video testimonials, sitting down with clients, It takes time. It takes time. And for you to post that film, edit that, and then see the returns from it, it can take weeks. Whereas a screenshot, a WhatsApp message, or something that you just found up on Canva, that can get you up in seconds.

Miles: Yeah. But again, like we're saying, this this speed thing with AI and everything else, if you're in the people business, which personal training, I still hope and I believe is, You've gotta build trust in the marketplace through genuine results with genuine people over a period of time. If you're just doing made-up screenshots and stuff like that- Do you think that's why a lot of PTs struggle? Because they're not doing the hard yards with their marketing. Josh: I think they struggle with that, but I think as well a lot of it is they're putting in little efforts but expecting- get a lot out of it. Yeah, it's almost like a basic math function machine. If you put in 2, you can't expect to get 4 back. Miles: It's just never gonna

Callum: happen. I think that's the problem though, right? Because we were saying this earlier, when you invite AI into your business, if you've already got substance, you're just trying to augment and make things run a little bit more smoothly. So again, with clients, maybe it's setting up something as simple as ManyChat. So when someone comments or said something, it's easier to get in contact. That bit I get. But when you're generating AI pictures, when you're trying to automate everything and put an AI bot doing this and that, but you've not even done the first success of making your business work yourself. Because only when it outgrows you should you look at really that upgrade. But if you've not had those wins yet, you can't prove the concept of what you're doing is working.

Miles: What would you do then? So as a new coach, newly qualified, if you were mentoring them to help them grow their business with their brand, their marketing, their social media, what would you take them through? Imagine just qualified today, what would you be sort of saying to us? First 3 things.

Josh: I can give you a real-time example of what we're working on. with BT Launch Lab, I've got like 3 or 4 calls booked in, one of which we've just done the exact same thing. So the first thing we're doing is always look at who you're actually delivering the service to. Now a lot of coaches, especially in this early stage that they're in, they think that the niche is a prison. They think that boxing their their client down is like, I can't say that because it's not relevant. The whole idea with who you deliver the service to, it is the root of the business. So let's just say If you don't understand, then you just you've got your qualifications, you just go out there, here I am, buy my services.

Josh: The problem with that is if you've got 500 followers and they all range from different age ranges, your content is not going to understand the conversations. So if you don't have an issue, you don't understand who you're delivering a service to, and you do a piece of content that is how to get to the gym early in the morning or how to wake up on time, that can't land because an 18-year-old, a 50-year-old, and a 90-year-old Which are all people on social media. They have different needs, different lifestyles, different circumstances. How can they connect to this content? So that goes back to you have to focus on who you deliver the service to. It doesn't necessarily have to be a person. Josh: It's if anything, it's more the pain point, because the pain point, you know, people can have.

Callum: When you talk about niche, this is a this is a question a lot of people ask, especially us. People find niching is, like you say, they're really narrowing down their audience. But there's so many different types of niches, right? You know, you see it very common online when people try to niche down. I want to work with busy busy men over 30 professionals. It's like, well, you're actually making that more broad than you think because then you've got a question who you think is professional. Yeah. You know, I want to work with mums and dads over 30. That's like 70% of the population. Like it's not a niche. Whereas when you're trying to try to find a new niche, how do you, how would you do it as a new coach? Callum: Because there's so many options. How do you relate it?

Josh: Absolutely. The thing that I'm big on is niche down on the problem and not the person. Because if you niche down on the person, which is busy men over 30 or an interesting one just to call out, it becomes Quite insulting is people will go for the busy professionals, men that are over 30 because they assume that they have money and they assume they can charge more because of it. You'll be surprised how much your average person, if you have a good service that actually produces results and it solves a pain point, people will pay money. People have money. But back to my original point, it's niching down on a problem, not a person. What happens if you say, I coach people aged 30 to 50 that like F1?

Josh: What if someone then comes to you and they're 29 years old? Are you just gonna be like, sorry mate, you're not 30 years old? Of course you're gonna coach them. Whereas if you focus on the pain point, you can be accessible to more people. It ticks the box of getting groundwork in with multiple people. You develop your people skills, communication, and you're still having a service that solves a specific problem. Because you're not- it's never- nobody wakes up and thinks, you know what, I want a personal trainer. You wake up and think, you know what, I want to be able to look at myself in the mirror. I want to be able to fit into a certain pair of jeans. Josh: I want to be able to go on holiday and be a better father. It's these problems, you're in the business of problem solving.

Callum: With your experience as a mentor, have you ever turned away potential coaches before? Josh: Absolutely. I think one of the best things is saying no to people and having tough conversations. The reason why I The reason I would personally turn someone away is one, their attitude to the programme itself. So one of the first things is somebody asks me how much it costs, I'm generally not gonna entertain that conversation. Or if I am, I hold my clients to a high standard because if they don't get the results or if they fail, it's gonna look bad on me. So if somebody is not prepared to do the work or if they're right off the bat looking for shortcuts, how long can you expect to get clients from this? What's the return?

Callum: Even in this age though, like, my only argument to that is people, it's the trust thing again, right? And you're doing the same job every personal trainer, coach, provider's doing. We're trying to establish trust. It's still always gonna come down to money. And obviously I know that you prove that by providing. But what traits What do you look for in your potential clients that you're going to raise as coaches that you would probably say, I don't think you're gonna make it?

Josh: I think it's because a lot of what I do is done-for-you consulting. So whenever I will teach you something, as long as it's not related to the coaching, I go ahead and do it. But when you learn a new piece of information, is new information learned, how quickly can I change your behaviour? So if I'm teaching you something, and a lot of coaches, a lot of general people who struggle to let their ego go because I've always done it this way and it's worked for me, but if it didn't work for you- so I think one of the things as well is I'll teach you stuff, but the implementation of it, the willingness just to let go of your old ideas and start thinking new ways would be a big

Callum: thing. Yeah, I get it, because the problem is I've turned learners away before, and I always look for something when I'm having a conversation with them. If I ask why you want to be a PT, If in within 3 word like sentences and 3 reasons, if it's not I want to help people, I know that they're not gonna do that well because that should be your first job. If your first thing is I want to go out there and make money, you're gonna struggle because the work comes in from you doing the hard rounds. I had a conversation with a potential earlier today. He already qualified but he wanted some mentorship and he asked me what am I doing because I qualified in January and I've got no clients.

Callum: Like, what are you doing now? Yeah. Says, well, I've had 3 potential clients, 1 ghosted me and 2 that I worked with just never got back to me. Says, well, what are you posting on social media? I've got a social media. Okay, are you posting? Not every day. Says, are you talking about it to people at work? Are you telling everybody about your business all the time? Are you asking people to come to the gym with you? Are you doing any free sessions? Like, the first year in PT I did, I must have done 60 hours free sessions. Just to build up that clientele, that testimonial graph. I think what people do is they go in with the money aspect.

Callum: If it's not worthwhile to them in the first 3 months, it's not gonna work. And that's that's what I mean with even your clients, your mentors that you're trying to bring through. Those traits will show pretty much straight away, right? Because they've been qualified for a while. And what they're doing now isn't working. They're not willing to Listen, there's a gap there.

Josh: I agree. Again, it's those old-school marketing techniques. One of the best things that I did when I was on the gym floor, 3 free, sits on a twister, 3 free PT sessions. Strip a piece of paper, you don't need any fancy systems. Name, email, contact number. Pin it up on the wall when they come in. You'll be booked out for weeks. It's just these simple things, but again, because it's like, well, I've gotta give something, I can't see that instant return straight away, I'm just not gonna do it. Because somebody either online has told me this or it just doesn't align. I don't think that's gonna give me a return. Sometimes what you think can run the business versus what actually will grow the business could be two very, very different things.

Josh: And you've got the coaches that will drop that there and then and they'll adapt and they'll pivot. You've also got the coaches that will be stiff, rigid. And if anything, I usually find it's the older coaches that are more resilient and they're open. These newer coaches, these new qualified PTs, they're so hungry, they're so willing to just do whatever it Callum: takes. Do you think that's because they're not willing to accept the new world that we're living in? Because it's vastly different from even 5 years ago. Like, it's not the same world. Like, there were things that you have to learn and be conscious of. Even social media now, you know, the way people are attacking it. It's more about volume and getting to the right person, right? But if people aren't willing to consider social media as one of their lead generation systems, they're gonna struggle.

Miles: Do you remember, you just went back to the the piece of paper analogy. And back in the late '90s when I started and got qualified as a PT, I remember A4 clipboard, piece of paper, speaking to people on the gym floor. What is he what is he what is What he what is he is it you're currently struggling with? And writing down and basically looking at what were the common pain points of members in the gym. Nowadays, a PT can actually do that. That's all your pieces of content for the week. What do people struggle with? But I still don't- I've just been to a gym before here and trained, and I was at 2 gyms in Cheshire on Friday.

Miles: And when I watch PTs in the gym, I'll see them hanging around reception. I still very rarely see them walking the floor and engaging, helping. What are you struggling with? If there's one thing I could give you, a magic wand to solve that problem, what would it be? Do you think that the art of speaking to people has has gone? Josh: 100%. Communication, because again, online coaching, you can- there's very successful coaches that will never see their clients in person. That person-to-person touchpoint engagement is completely obsolete when it comes to online coaching, which I think is a problem in the space.

Callum: Do you not feel like though your communication should be, if not double what you're doing on the gym floor anyway? Because we're living in an age now where some don't want to respond to text for 48 hours. As a coach, your relationship with your client is completely electronic, and you have to give them what they need, and you might not speak to them for a few days. Like on the gym floor, if you are seeing your client 3 times a week, you've got to report to the point where you're spending half of that session just catching up. But the online coach

Josh: hasn't got that time. It's very to the point, right? Yeah, it's just we've lost that relationship aspect, and it almost seems like You've gotta remember my entire business, a large part of it is helping online coaches and PTs. So it's not like we're taking this down the segue of saying online coaching is bad. But there is definitely a good, even like a USP to be had of just increasing that communication aspect.

Miles: The stuff that you would see in a personal trainer in a successful in-person business can absolutely be transferred online. Just, you know, instead of sending a WhatsApp message, just pick the phone and call them. Having weekly calls and set the expectation from the start. You'll learn more about a client in a 60-minute call than you will a week on dial with a phone, back and forth, or some messages. So you said number 1 is looking for the problem. The first thing. What would you say is the next thing?

Josh: The way that you can communicate that online. If you're trying to get clients online, you simply have to be where your audience is congregating. So it's one thing, right, you figured out who you're actually delivering the service to, but so far this idea just exists in your mind. And again, to get it out of your mind and be able to communicate that is a completely different conversation to begin with. Because then that opens up the door into what you're saying when it comes to your content, how you're posting that content. So the main thing now is being able to communicate that message. I've seen coaches where they've got a really good bio. They've got- I can land on their page and know exactly who they coach, but then I'll go through the content and it's still just the generic stuff.

Josh: So it's understanding the root of your business, but now you've gotta be able to communicate that to the rest of the Miles: world. So so basically when when I land on a PT's page, what you're saying, you should clearly be able to look through it and understand what they're about, who they help, and what problems they solve. That's that's basically what about number 3, what's the next thing?

Josh: Tell them what to do. The best way that I do this is when it comes to marketing is in a non-condescending and sort of way. Always treat your audience and your followers either like they're stupid, a 3-year-old, or completely from outer space. So if you do it, you'll be surprised how many PTs and coaches think, you know, they're sulking because they haven't got clients, they're stressed, they're in a period now where they haven't got clients. Clients come in, but they're not telling people what to do because they're running on assumption. "I've done the course, I've done the targeted stuff, I've figured out who I'm coaching, I understand what I'm doing." When was the last time you told them to actually do something?

Josh: If you've got something of free value, if you want to do an M B T, a call, a recipe book, a lead magnet, but tell them to actually download it. It is very much a relationship. Miles: Tell them the next step. Josh: Tell them the next step. Tell them what to do. You can't have We've all got misses, I assume. None of us are mind readers, right? It functions well when we either get them to tell us what they want us to do or vice versa. We don't assume. Callum: I don't know about yours, but mine gets mad when I ask her to tell me what to do. Josh: Yeah, because then you go- Callum: I ask for the direct solution, she just gets mad. Josh: Yeah, because why didn't you know what to do? Miles: You should know me by now. Josh: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

Miles: Yeah, so tell them what to do is number 3. Another thing I wanted to ask you, Josh, is And this this is I think this is a big problem that I think a lot of PTs out there will align with is I I think and I think I might be not far off the mark with this. I think PTs are scared sometimes of putting content out there and they might think, "I can't say that, I can't post that," because they're scared of the opinions of others. And when I say others, What I mean by that is they're scared of what other coaches and trainers will comment on their post. But that is not their ideal client. Miles: So their opinion is is largely irrelevant. Now, do you see PTs who say, "I don't know what to- I daren't say that." Do you get that?

Josh: Absolutely, yeah. You see it as well sometimes the more qualified the coach is. So I know this coach, I won't name and glorify. He is a fantastic coach. He's invested thousands into his education, he's paid for mentors, and yet he's constantly starting from scratch. He's barely got any clients, he's always having to start from ground zero with his business. But yet if I look at his following and the stories that he's posting, he's posting to other coaches. This is where the root of the problem lies. You're creating content for other coaches and not for clients. There is a there's a razor sharp line as to how different it is. Because coaches, likes, comments, it's all just a monopoly in your mind that exists.

Josh: But we think that because we're in this little universe that everybody knows about it. But you'll be surprised how you talking about resistance profiles on the machine or the latest trend, we've got Jordan Peters that's back now, everybody's losing their mind over it. Yeah. But we assume again, assuming, because of It's not because of our ideas that just everybody knows it. So again, this idea of other coaches' opinions, one, it's an internal thing you've just gotta work on, and two, they don't pay the bills. Go try pay your mortgage or car payment with the other opinion of another coach.

Callum: I think it's easy to get caught in that trap though, because we're in an age of controversy now, where if you are a coach and then you see your role model coaches Blasting on other coaches and it's just a back and forth thing. 'Cause usually it's gotta be an unpopular opinion to go viral. Yeah. It's gotta be something being outlandish saying something. And I think the idea of going viral and getting clients obviously to be a good thing. But what would put a new PT off is now we're living in an age where if you see someone so deep into their content where they're posting 3, 4 times a day, it's more natural to them. I can understand why that coach would be reluctant to post because it's when they think they haven't got the ideas to put on there, they think it's irrelevant.

Callum: But I think everyone's like that. Like you say, they jump on trends and stuff like that. But the real coaches who are making real impacts, like you say, are not caring about having negative opinions. Because if you've got no enemies, you're not doing enough. But if you've got no haters, you're not doing it good enough. You've gotta go out there and say how how you view it, even if it's controversial. Miles: Hate hate never comes from above, does it? Callum: Yeah, you're always punching down.

Miles: It's always coming from below. So I I think coaches over the years that I've spoken to, even even gym owners who daren't say things. But it's like if you can solve a problem for your target audience in your target local area, What other gyms say about you is like it's irrelevant. You've gotta be able to put yourself out there in spite of the the opinions, the criticisms of others. How do you think a PT would get over that fear?

Josh: It's always, you're always a laughingstock until you actually pull it off. And again, you do all of this work and then all of a sudden it's like you're an overnight success. It's not about the bottle. It's the, you know, the looking like a little bit of a joke, maybe you're doing on trend or whatever it is, just simply being uncomfortable. Like me, I'm a very laid-back, reserved person. I'm part of my marketing strategy. I'll never be doing TikTok dances or anything like that, but if I've got something to say, I will say that. And sometimes that means doing maybe even like a live video. This is my first podcast that I've ever been on in a live environment.

Josh: So it's again going into those unknown things because you know- Which sounds obviously really cheesy, you know, you just got to do what makes you uncomfortable, but if there's truth in it, why not just action anyway? Miles: So exposure therapy, just keep doing it until it becomes less painful and it becomes more natural. Josh: Yeah, no one's tired of it. I've recently heard that. It's good when you- you know, it's painful when you're not getting clients. Nobody wants to send the emails, the outreach messages, following, doing the boring stuff. But the second you get, yeah, I have some money, let's get on call, and that actual yes, you're humbling.

Callum: Yeah, I think- yeah, I mean, I got told an interesting thing the other day. You've got a failing business until it's successful. Doesn't matter if you've got 3 clients, 2 clients, Until whatever you deem successful, which is a really important point. Like, what is your idea of success? Is your idea being financially free? Is your idea of having a brand? Is your idea- whatever that is, until you get that, it's a failing business. And a failing business is not a done and done business. You just work on it constantly. And I think what people are scared of is making failures, right? And having slip- Hiccups and stuff in business. You need to make those failures because they're gonna teach you a lesson and you're gonna learn something.

Callum: But we live in an age now where we just set it for- we turned it on about AI. They want to be there instantly. They want to be making money instantly. But if you're gonna zip forward and miss out all those critical lessons, what are you gonna do when you get to that point and the next hurdle comes? And you haven't learned the thing that you need to learn to be able to deal with it.

Josh: It's like ManyChat you touched on, and I have a personal- it's not like I have beef with it, but I'm definitely not a fan of the platform. You'll see a coach with like 7,000 followers, or even you'll see coaches and you know, a lot of influencers, wherever it comes from, a couple hundred thousand followers, and then they'll set up a ManyChat. In its place, in the right circumstance, for sure, if you've got hundreds of comments coming through, hundreds of messages. It has its place. But you'll see a coach with several thousand followers have a ManyChat automation in place when they do a callout saying, "DM me the word freebie," and 2 people say, "Why on earth would you need ManyChat for that?" The skill set that you need to learn from that is how do you actually send that first message?

Josh: It's email marketing, it's marketing. So what can you send in that first line of that DM to get someone to open that DM to begin with? If you're just jumping straight to that ManyChat because you assume that it works and it's what the other coaches, more followers than you, are doing, you're missing that vital step of yet again human interaction, which is sending that first message. Miles: If you don't know what that natural back and forwards is, your automations will never sound natural, will they? Because later on, if you've never actually done those automations over a period of time, back and forth, you kind of know the natural flow of a conversation. Whereas if you do an AI automation from the start with no experience, it just sounds fake, doesn't it?

Callum: And people are picking up on it fast now. I'm not seeing that as much anymore. And I think people are starting to sniff it out. I mean, uh, James Smith and a few other coaches do it, about the honesty, being upfront about it, saying, if you comment this, my ManyChat's gonna send you this, but it's gonna be valuable because it's a good book or it's a good PDF. Miles: It's not gonna be me at 3 o'clock in the morning within 2 seconds replying.

Callum: And I liked it because I think what we're missing out on key marketing things, and this is good for personal trainers to hear. I don't know if you agree, but being honest about your marketing, saying, you know, click this button, I'm gonna send you 3 emails, by that 3 emails you'll probably want to have a conversation, and they're gonna be in a chain, aren't they? Because everyone knows what an email is now, you know, you're going to pop, like, be honest about it because the clients that you try and speak to, as long as you're honest with them, I feel like there's gonna be some communication there.

Josh: It reminds me, and this is completely resourceful when it comes to coaches wanting to outreach and figure out how you send that first message, you know, coming to making the first move. But one of the biggest things that will help is addressing the elephant in the room. So when I'm speaking to a coach and this means to send the first message, or I'm getting my clients and I'm upskilling them If you're messaging someone that follows you, they've liked a couple of photos, you don't just want to be going in on like, "Hey bro, how's training?" One of the easiest opening lines I'll say in a voice note is, "Appreciate this sounds like a little bit like a spam message," or "I understand you probably get a lot of these messages." Just by addressing that, you're creating that common ground of you both know that it's two strangers talking to one another.

Miles: Yeah. That honestly helps create common ground. Yeah, that makes perfect sense. What do you see when you look at profiles of PTs and online coaches? What do you see as- you almost want to put your hands over your eyes and not look at them. What do you see that is common, what we would say mistakes or don't help people grow the business? What do you see people posting badly? Josh: I would say generic messaging is a thing I see all the time, but more so, more better than that is bios that sound like CVs. People think that when you become a personal trainer, and I see this a lot more that I'm starting to work with US clients as well, is they'll have just a list of credentials. They've done the bachelor's, the master's, level 2, level 3. Miles: Pre and postnatal.

Josh: Yeah, yeah. And it's like, I've worked a lot of sales jobs in the past, I've always got a Personal training and sales are very, very compatible things. One of the first things that you'll learn, page 3 of any sales book, is features versus benefits. Feature is what something does. The benefit is how it actually helps someone. faqs.q: Should a newly qualified PT go straight into online coaching?
faqs.a: Josh doesn't think so. The online coaching space isn't regulated, and time on the gym floor is one of the best things a new trainer can do: it builds people skills and shows you what you are actually good at.

faqs.q: How should a new personal trainer choose a niche?
faqs.a: Josh's rule is to "niche down on the problem and not the person". Nobody wakes up wanting a personal trainer; they want to fit into a pair of jeans or feel confident on holiday. Focusing on a problem keeps you accessible to more people than picking an age group or job title.

faqs.q: What should a personal trainer put in their Instagram bio?
faqs.a: Not a list of qualifications. Josh says bios that read like CVs are one of the most common mistakes. Your bio should say what problem you solve, what you help people achieve, and what they should do next.

faqs.q: How should a PT with only a few hours a week spend their marketing time?
faqs.a: Mostly on making the first move. Josh says there are three ways to get clients: pay for them, wait for them, or start conversations yourself. He recommends personal voice notes using the person's name rather than copy-and-paste DMs.

faqs.q: Where do personal trainers get enquiries from on Instagram?
faqs.a: Josh says enquiries mostly come from stories. Instead of posting and moving on, turn one feed post into three to five stories: ask a question, add some social proof, then finish with a sticker call to action.

faqs.q: Should new PTs use AI and automation tools like ManyChat?
faqs.a: Josh says AI makes you more of what you already are, so it won't fix a business that isn't working. Tools like ManyChat have their place once you have hundreds of comments, but new trainers should learn to send the first message themselves.
